title: Depart content
hookLine: Marcus ends: go gladly, for the one who dismisses you is gracious (Meditations 12.36)

lines: THE LAST LINE OF A BOOK.
cards: The last line of a book carries weight. Readers remember it. Writers sweat over it.
Marcus wrote his notebook to himself, so we can't be sure he chose his last line.

But the passage that stands at the end, as the book has come down to us, is about a stage, an actor, and a man in charge of the show who says: that's enough, you can go. It's about death, and it's surprisingly gentle.

teach.h: THE ACTOR WITH THREE ACTS DONE.
teach.b: First, the scene. In 12.36 Marcus pictures a comic actor whom the official in charge of the games dismisses from the stage. The actor protests: but I've only played three of the five acts.

The answer comes back, in effect: in life, three acts can be the whole play. The one who put the drama together decides when it's complete, and the one who ends it does too. You were the cause of neither.
Second, the line itself, in George Long's translation: "Depart then satisfied, for he also who releases thee is satisfied."
The Greek word Long renders satisfied is hileōs, which also means gracious, kindly, at peace.
So you could hear it both ways: go at peace, because the one releasing you is at peace with you; go gladly, because you're being dismissed kindly, not thrown out. Third, who that one is.

teach.h: WHO RELEASES YOU? NATURE, HE SAYS.
teach.b: Earlier in the same passage, Marcus names it: not a tyrant or an unjust judge sends you off the stage, but nature, the same nature that brought you onto it.
Elsewhere he also speaks of the whole, of God, of the gods. Some readers hear a personal God here; some hear nature itself, the order of things. The text leaves room for both.
Fourth, why it's for the living. Every day ends before you've finished everything. Every job, every season, every conversation gets called before act five.
Marcus's last word is practice for the small endings: leave the stage without clutching the curtain.

how: Readers often treat the last passage of the Meditations as an evening practice, ending the day as a complete act rather than an unfinished one.

o: leave quickly, before anyone can ask you to stay longer
leave only once every task in your life is finished
leave at peace, since the one who releases you is at peace

p: dismissed after three of five acts

s: Marcus clearly planned 12.36 as the ending of a published book
he wrote to himself; we can't be sure he chose a last line, but this passage ends the book as it has come down to us.
the last line has the actor told that three acts can be the whole play
the one who put the drama together decides when it's complete.
in 12.36 a tyrant or an unjust judge sends us off the stage
Marcus says it's nature, the same nature that brought us on; readers hear that religiously or naturally.

games.q: you're the actor, pulled off the stage after act three. what does the last passage of the Meditations invite you to do?
o: argue for your last two acts.
go at peace, since the one who releases you is at peace.
games.why: Marcus ends with the actor going satisfied, because the one who dismisses him is gracious. it's practice for every small ending, too.

practice: Think of today as a play with acts, and name the ones already done, some that went well, some that didn't, and anything you're still clutching.
Then picture today's curtain, a few hours from now, and if you can, let today be complete as it is, three acts or five, and enough.

wordCard.voice: Depart content. The last words of the Meditations: leave the stage at peace, because the one who releases you is at peace too. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: gracious, kindly, at peace. Used twice in the last sentence of the Meditations: go hileōs, for the one who releases you is hileōs.

carryVoice: Your line: go gladly. You're being dismissed kindly, not thrown out of the play. Rest well tonight.
